title: Final: strings, enums, arrays
sub: String comparison, allocation-free building, flags, covariance and int?
cards/0/q: Which calls compare using the current culture by default? Select all.
cards/0/explain: == and Contains are ordinal. StartsWith(string), Compare and sorting through Comparer<string>.Default use the thread culture, and with ICU or tr-TR the result can surprise you.
cards/1/q: A cache key is built as url.ToLower(). On servers with the tr-TR culture some requests miss the cache. Which fix is right?
cards/1/options/0: url.ToLowerInvariant() or a dictionary with StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase
cards/1/options/3: Compare keys with string.Compare(a, b, true)
cards/1/explain: In tr-TR "I" turns into the dotless "ı", and the keys drift apart. Identifiers are compared without language rules. Intern does not change the text, ToUpper breaks on the same letter, and Compare with ignoreCase still depends on the culture.
cards/1/wrong/3: The Compare(a, b, ignoreCase) overload still uses the current culture.
cards/2/q: id is an int, name is a string. What does C# 12 turn $"{id}: {name}" into?
cards/2/options/0: DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler: AppendFormatted(id) without boxing, one result string
cards/2/options/1: string.Format with an object[] and boxing of id
cards/2/options/2: A StringBuilder with three Append calls
cards/2/options/3: string.Concat(id, ": ", name) with boxing of id
cards/2/explain: Since C# 10 and .NET 6 interpolation goes through a ref struct handler with a buffer from ArrayPool. AppendFormatted<T> is generic, so the int is written straight into the buffer. string.Format was the pre-C# 10 way.
cards/3/q: Match the construct with what is behind it
cards/3/pairs/2/1: A type check on every store
cards/4/q: enum Light { Red, Yellow, Green }. A method is a switch expression with arms for the three names and no _. What happens on Act((Light)7)?
cards/4/options/0: SwitchExpressionException; the compiler warned with CS8524 in advance
cards/4/options/2: It does not compile: (Light)7 is out of range
cards/4/options/3: The Green arm runs as the last one
cards/4/explain: An enum is the whole int range; the names are just points in it. The compiler warns about unnamed values, and the generated code throws SwitchExpressionException when no arm matches.
cards/5/q: A default value without an exception, and parsing with a check that the member is declared
cards/5/explain: .Value throws InvalidOperationException when there is no value. TryParse also accepts "42", so the IsDefined after it is not redundant.
cards/6/q: What is true about arrays? Select all.
cards/6/options/0: Rows of a jagged array can have different lengths
cards/6/options/1: int[,] is a single heap object
cards/6/options/4: int[] a = []; does not create a new array
cards/6/explain: Only arrays of reference types are covariant. InlineArray is the safe alternative to a fixed buffer. An empty collection expression for an array is the shared Array.Empty<int>().
cards/7/q: Which line throws at run time?
cards/7/explain: Storing a string and null into a string[] is legal. A ReadOnlySpan does not allow writes, so covariance does not hurt it. A Span<object> could write a non-string there — its constructor sees that the array is really a string[] and throws ArrayTypeMismatchException.
cards/8/q: Public library: enum Level { Low, High }. In v2 they want to add Medium, which logically sits between them. How do you avoid breaking consumers that are already built?
cards/8/options/0: Keep Low = 0, High = 1 and add Medium = 2 at the end
cards/8/options/1: Insert Medium in the middle: the names did not change
cards/8/options/2: Turn Level into a class with static fields
cards/8/explain: Consumers keep numbers in their IL, not names. Inserting in the middle moves High from 1 to 2, and old code starts mixing up levels. New members go only at the end, with explicit values.
